Canada has officially launched its Real-Time Rail Monday (Nov. 9), introducing around-the-clock payment infrastructure designed to accelerate money movement, improve cash flow management and give financial institutions and payment providers a platform for developing new services.

The system uses the ISO 20022 messaging standard to support richer transaction information and is designed to give businesses and consumers faster access to funds and greater visibility into their finances.

The economic implications could be substantial. The C.D. Howe Institute estimates that the system could generate up to $14.5 billion in cost savings and $16 billion in broader economic gains, potentially rising to $27 billion as additional capabilities are introduced.

Security is another central component of the rollout. Canada is the first G7 country to launch a real-time payments system with mandatory centralized fraud services in place from day one, according to Payments Canada. Those protections include confirmation of payee, transaction safety scoring and centralized fraud intelligence sharing.

The initial group of participants includes Wealthsimple, Questbank, Peoples Trust Company, Paramount Commerce, KOHO, DoBusiness.com, Digital Commerce Bank and Bank of America.

Payments Canada expects additional financial institutions and payment providers to join in the coming months, with the system projected to reach more than 90% of Canadians within its first year.

Demand for faster payments is also evident among businesses and consumers. Payments Canada research found that 60% of Canadian businesses are prepared to adopt real-time payments to address operational challenges, including cash flow forecasting and payment delays. Another 52% of surveyed consumers expressed interest and intent to use the services.

For businesses, immediate access to incoming funds could improve liquidity management and reduce the need to maintain cash reserves while payments clear. For consumers, the system promises greater control over when money moves and becomes available.

The launch gives Canadian financial institutions and FinTechs a shared foundation for developing new payment products and services as the country modernizes its national payments infrastructure.

title: Global Payments faces industry pricing pressure
snippet: While analysts point to an increasingly competitive environment for the processor, the company is still trying to raise prices.
fullText:
Global Payments and other processors face an increasingly competitive market, with rising pricing pressures forcing some businesses in the ecosystem to consider consolidation.

Global Payments has touted increased merchant acceptance of its Genius point-of-sale services brand, but now it may be trying to force through price hikes in an increasingly competitive market.

The payments processing company is seeking to implement a new $699 annual fee for its merchant clients next month, according to a merchant consultant who posted a portion of a Global Payments letter on LinkedIn. 

“Worldpay, now part of Global Payments, is introducing a $699 annual fee, with the first charge hitting merchant statements this December. Yes, another one,” Merchant Cost Consulting Partner Matt Rej said in the LinkedIn post last week. “And this is on top of the other increases we've already seen from Worldpay this year.”

Rej questioned, and poked fun at, the reasoning Global Payments provided for the increase, pointing to the company’s letter saying: “Government and industry regulations have had a significant impact on system requirements in the payment processing industry.”

The Atlanta-based company didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment. Nonetheless, in its third-quarter earnings press release last week, the company acknowledged “increased competition in the markets in which we operate.”

Global Payments pricing moves come less than a year after it completed its $24.25 billion purchase of the merchant services company Worldpay, which could give the company stronger pricing power in the industry. In the third-quarter report, Global Payments reported that the Genius brand, which was launched last year, was placed at 65% more merchant locations, compared to the year-earlier period, and bookings more than doubled.   

As the Genius brand gains traction, the company is reportedly considering selling itself off to one of its largest shareholders, private equity firm GTCR, and the investment firm Clayton, Dubilier & Rice. GTCR is acquainted with Global Payments partly because it was one of the companies that sold it the Worldpay assets.

Any fee increases by POS service providers are increasingly met with pressure from younger financial technology companies building a presence in the market with newer technologies. As a result, some legacy companies that provide payments services to merchants, including behemoth Fiserv, the new entrant Shift4 and the Dutch company Adyen, are feeling a competitive crunch.

Point-of-sale services firm PayCompass said in September that it had merged with two other firms and the CEO at the merchant services provider Butter Payments said last month that the company had sold its assets to an unnamed buyer.

While analysts who follow Global Payments praised the company’s progress in integrating Worldpay into its operations and luring merchants to the Genius brand, they noted the increasingly competitive market. As such, price increases may be a tough sell, particularly as merchants face consumers stretched by inflationary pressures. 

Analysts at the investment firm William Blair raised concerns about Global Payments technology being capable of competing with new fintechs.

“While sales metrics appear strong, we argue Genius is simply not a competitive offering from a technology standpoint and will not become material enough to durably accelerate consolidated organic growth,” the analysts said in a Thursday note to their clients, acknowledging the brand’s third-quarter growth.

Other analysts who follow the company also pointed out the competitive intensity in the market in commenting on Global Payments results.

“The Payments industry is very competitive with both existing and emerging competition,” analysts for TD Cowen told clients in a note Thursday. “All of our companies face the risk of being unable to capture market share or having their business models become commoditized by newer entrants in the market. Additionally, our companies are levered to consumer spending and therefore are exposed to general economic conditions.”

Analysts who follow the company for the investment firm R.W. Baird called out the difficulties for raising prices at this time across the industry. “Pricing pressure is a constant threat, and new fintechs have become competitive threats as well,” analysts at the Baird Equity Research arm said in a Thursday note. 

A sale to private owners might relieve some of the pressure of operating in the publicly traded market, with its focus on quarterly reports. Still, the analysts at William Blair last week gave the deal less than a 50-50 chance of being completed, partly because of the debt that Global Payments has in the wake of its Worldpay deal.

In a prior Oct. 30 note focused exclusively on the reports of a potential Global Payments sale, the William Blair analysts said that some $22 billion of debt at the company “could be an impediment, especially in a rising rate environment.”

The William Blair analysts posited that they could be wrong about the chances of the sale. If they are, they forecast that other “debt-laden” publicly traded companies in the industry, including Shift4 Payments and Fiserv, “pressure to sell will ratchet up dramatically, setting up what could be the final wave of industry consolidation.”

title: TotallyMoney Hits Six Million Users as Credit-Score Habits Drive Gains
snippet: The free credit app said one-in-ten UK adults have now used its service, with monthly checkers recording a 133% larger score improvement than The post TotallyMoney Hits Six Million Users as Credit-Score Habits Drive Gains appeared first on The Fintech Times.
fullText:
TotallyMoney, the free credit report and score app operated by Intelligent Lending Group, has reached six million registered users in the UK, a milestone the Manchester-based company marked on 21 October 2026. The figure represents roughly 11% of the UK adult population, based on mid-2025 ONS population data cited by the company.

The platform provides users with live access to their TransUnion credit score and report, alongside automated alerts when the score changes and personalised guidance on improving their credit standing. It also acts as a lead-generation channel for credit cards, loans and other retail financial products, a model common among UK credit-comparison and credit-health platforms.

What the engagement data shows

Nik Charalampous, CEO at TotallyMoney

TotallyMoney’s internal analysis of more than 7,000 customers who joined in September 2025 and were tracked through to July 2026 found that 45% of those who started with a “low” TransUnion score (below 556) improved their score within six months. Among the lowest-scoring segment, customers who entered with a score below 400, the proportion who improved was 86%.

Frequency of use correlated strongly with outcome. Customers who checked their report every month achieved a score increase 2.3 times, or 133%, larger on average than those who engaged less regularly. The company attributes this to habitual monitoring prompting behaviour changes: paying down balances, correcting errors on a report, or simply avoiding missed payments. The analysis is self-reported and conducted by TotallyMoney’s own data team rather than an independent third party, a caveat worth noting.

Chief executive Nik Charalampous described the milestone as the result of people taking active control of their financial situations, and pointed to the breadth of circumstances driving sign-ups, ranging from thin-file consumers without an established UK credit record to those rebuilding after financial difficulty or preparing for a major credit commitment such as a mortgage.

Market context and competitive landscape

The UK credit-health market has matured considerably since TotallyMoney launched its free credit report service in 2017. Credit Karma, Experian‘s consumer app, ClearScore and MoneySuperMarket‘s credit tools compete for similar audiences, and all operate on variants of the same freemium model: offer free credit monitoring, monetise through matched product recommendations. The competitive advantage tends to sit in data depth, matching accuracy and the quality of the personalisation engine rather than in the report itself, since TransUnion, Equifax and Experian data is accessible across platforms.

For lenders, the segment matters because users who actively monitor their credit tend to be better-informed borrowers, and platforms that can demonstrate measurable score improvement have a stronger commercial proposition when negotiating referral or white-label arrangements with credit providers. TotallyMoney’s six-million-user figure positions it as a credible data asset within the Intelligent Lending Group portfolio alongside Binq, CredAbility, Ocean and Luv Cars.

The UK’s financial inclusion agenda adds a policy dimension. The FCA has placed increased emphasis on consumer understanding of credit and the fair treatment of customers in financial difficulty. Platforms that can show measurable credit-score improvement among thin-file or recovering borrowers align with that agenda, even if they sit outside the FCA’s direct regulatory perimeter as credit brokers rather than lenders. As open finance obligations develop under the broader Data and Smart Data Bill framework, credit-health apps will also be positioned to ingest a richer data set, which could deepen the personalisation that drives the engagement numbers cited here.

title: Piston Brings Cardless Fleet Fuel Payments to 341 Jacksons Stores
snippet: The cardless fleet payment network is now live at all Jacksons Food Stores locations across eight western US states, expanding its merchant footprint. The post Piston Brings Cardless Fleet Fuel Payments to 341 Jacksons Stores appeared first on The Fintech Times.
fullText:
Piston, a Cupertino-based cardless payment network serving commercial fleets, has gone live at 341 Jacksons Food Stores locations across eight western US states. The rollout represents one of the larger single-partner expansions in the company’s history and takes Piston’s total merchant coverage to more than 3,000 fuel stations across 48 states.

The partnership gives fleet operators on Piston’s network additional fuelling options when planning routes in the western US, while Jacksons gains a channel to attract commercial fuel volume without adding a new card scheme or open-loop network. Piston replaces the physical fleet card with mobile authorisation tied to a specific driver and vehicle, giving fleet managers real-time spend visibility at the transaction level.

How the network model works

Piston’s commercial proposition rests on a direct integration at the point of sale rather than routing through the traditional card-network stack. The company says this removes four intermediaries from the standard transaction chain, improving the economics for both the fuel retailer and the fleet. Direct POS integration also gives Piston access to richer transaction data than an open-loop card network would see, which the company says underpins its fraud-prevention tooling.

That fraud layer now includes Piston Guard, a real-time tool that can flag or block suspected fraudulent purchases before settlement, and Piston Analytics Agent, which surfaces spending patterns for fleet operators. Both are positioned as AI-assisted capabilities, though the release did not provide performance benchmarks or third-party validation for either product.

Cory Jackson, president of Jacksons Food Stores, said that commercial fuelling is a meaningful part of the chain’s business and that the way fleets pay is shifting. “Working with Piston helps us keep pace with that shift and makes Jacksons a practical stop for fleets using modern payment technology,” he said.

Market context and competitive positioning

The US fleet card market is a well-established segment dominated by WEX, Fleetcor and Comdata, all of which operate large closed-loop or open-loop networks with deep integrations into fuel retailers and telematics providers. Piston’s bet is that a cardless, mobile-first network built on direct POS partnerships can undercut incumbents on cost and out-compete them on data granularity and fraud prevention.

The growth figures cited in the release are notable if accurate. Piston reported an eightfold increase in payment volume and a fortyfold expansion of its merchant network over the past year, though no base figures were provided, making the absolute scale difficult to assess. The company also noted that its POS integrations are certified on systems representing more than 95 percent of US merchant fuel sites, a figure that, if independently verified, would represent significant infrastructure coverage for a business of this age.

Piston closed a $15 million Series A round led by FPV Ventures earlier this year, with participation from existing backers Spark Capital and Pear VC, taking total funding to $22.5 million. The company said it intends to use that capital to onboard additional fuel retailers, expand product capabilities and grow headcount. At $22.5 million in total funding, Piston remains lightly capitalised relative to its stated ambitions. The pace of merchant network growth will be the clearest indicator of whether the direct-partnership model can scale before better-resourced incumbents respond.

FCA to explore quantum computing to tackle financial crime

              

  

  

  
    

        

    

      

A new initiative will bring together firms, quantum technology providers, and national research labs to explore practical applications of quantum computing.

  

            						

The FCA will bring together financial services firms, quantum technology providers and national research laboratories to explore how quantum computing could help tackle financial crime.

The Quantum Experimentation Group, the first of its kind for a regulator, will initially explore how quantum machine learning could help detect money laundering and fraud. It will launch in the first quarter of 2027.

Participants will use an FCA synthetic dataset – artificially generated data – to help overcome a key barrier to testing: access to suitable data.

The group will help firms explore practical uses of quantum computing in financial services and share findings to guide future testing. It will also help the FCA understand the technology’s opportunities and limitations, barriers to experimentation and what these could mean for regulation.

Jessica Rusu, chief data, information and intelligence officer at the FCA, said: 'We want to help firms explore where quantum could make a meaningful difference, and early experimentation is essential to understanding its potential in financial services. By bringing together firms, technology providers and researchers we can build readiness and identify practical applications for common industry challenges, starting with financial crime.'

The initiative builds on the FCA’s research into the long-term potential of quantum computing in financial services.

Financial services firms, quantum technology providers and national research laboratories can register their interest in joining the group by 31 December 2026.

Notes to editors

Read more about the Quantum Experimentation Group and how to register an interest in joining the group.

The FCA’s Quantum Experimentation Group will be the world’s first regulator-led quantum computing experimentation group.

The group will support organisations at different stages of their quantum journey, from those beginning to explore potential use cases to those already undertaking advanced experimentation.

As part of the initiative, the FCA will define problem statements and work alongside participants to build understanding of the opportunities, limitations and practical considerations associated with quantum technologies.

The initiative will complement wider activity across the UK’s quantum ecosystem by creating additional opportunities for collaborative experimentation and learning.

title: PayPal Urges Retailers to Show BNPL Earlier as Black Friday Nears
snippet: PayPal research finds 67% of Christmas BNPL shoppers are more likely to add items to their basket when payment options appear on product pages. The post PayPal Urges Retailers to Show BNPL Earlier as Black Friday Nears appeared first on The Fintech Times.
fullText:
PayPal has published research ahead of the Black Friday and Cyber Monday peak, warning UK retailers that late disclosure of buy now, pay later options is costing them basket additions. The payments group says nine in ten UK adults are actively managing festive spending, and that visibility of instalment-payment options earlier in the shopping journey can materially shift conversion.

The research, conducted by Morning Consult on behalf of PayPal between 4 and 10 September 2026 among 2,076 UK adults, found that more than half of Christmas BNPL shoppers (55%) would favour a retailer that shows the option on product pages over one that waits until the checkout step, where only 21% said they preferred to see it. Two-thirds (67%) said earlier visibility would make them more likely to add an item to their basket. PayPal also cited its own internal data showing an 11% uplift in PayPal payment volumes among merchants that introduced Pay Later messaging or a second checkout button, though it noted results may vary and the underlying merchant sample dated from March 2020 to September 2025.

The BNPL placement argument

The distinction between product-page and checkout-page disclosure is commercially significant. At checkout, a shopper has already decided in principle to buy; instalment framing at that point reduces friction but does not drive discovery. On the product page, showing a weekly or monthly cost alongside a headline price addresses affordability earlier, when the shopper is still deciding whether to proceed. For higher-consideration purchases, that reframing can be the deciding factor.

UK home fitness retailer JTX Fitness offered a case study in the release. Jamie Forshaw, head of marketing at JTX Fitness, said: “Showing customers their payment options while they’re still browsing can help them feel more confident about how they’ll manage the cost. When customers can see Pay Later from the product page onwards, more of them go from browsing to buying.”

Sean Douglas, senior director of UK Large Enterprise at PayPal, noted that peak season pressure tends to put retailers in survival mode, but argued the data pointed to a more active opportunity: the 11% volume uplift, he said, could be the difference between meeting revenue targets and exceeding them.

Market context and regulatory backdrop

PayPal’s Pay Later sits within a BNPL market that is under active regulatory review in the UK. The Financial Conduct Authority has been developing a framework to bring point-of-sale credit products within the Consumer Credit Act perimeter, a process that has run for several years and is expected to introduce affordability check requirements, clearer pre-contract disclosure rules and new marketing standards. Once the regime is live, the question of where and how BNPL options are surfaced to consumers will move from a commercial optimisation decision to a compliance one.

The broader market for embedded BNPL includes Klarna, Clearpay (Afterpay) and Zilch, each of which also promotes early product-page integration to merchant partners. PayPal’s advantage in this space is distribution: its existing merchant acceptance network and buyer-side login reduce integration friction compared with a standalone BNPL provider. The research release is also a vehicle for directing merchants to PayPal’s Pay Later onboarding page, so the findings should be read in that commercial context.

The AI finding is a secondary data point worth watching. More than a third of respondents (35%) said they had used or planned to use AI for Christmas shopping, and 52% said they would use it specifically to find deals or compare prices. If AI-assisted browsing compresses the product discovery phase, the window in which payment messaging can influence a shopper may shift again, adding further complexity to where in the journey BNPL should appear.

title: Pmtbox adds Coupons.com Founder Steven Boal to its Board
snippet: The Utah-based merchant payments platform said Boal brings two decades of fraud and payments infrastructure experience from Coupons.com and CashStar. The post Pmtbox adds Coupons.com Founder Steven Boal to its Board appeared first on The Fintech Times.
fullText:
pmtbox, the Utah-based enterprise commerce platform that consolidates payments, risk intelligence and transaction data for merchants, has appointed Steven Boal to its board of directors. Boal founded Quotient Technology, better known as Coupons.com, in 1998 and led it as chief executive and board chair for 24 years through its listing on the New York Stock Exchange. He also founded digital gifting firm CashStar, which was acquired by Blackhawk Network in 2017.

The appointment follows April’s $15 million seed round led by Tandem Ventures, reported at the time to be the largest seed raise in Utah in the past decade. Boal joins Tandem founding partner Alex Bean and pmtbox founder Wayne Hamilton on the board.

Experience where money changes hands

Boal’s relevance to pmtbox extends beyond capital markets credibility. At Coupons.com, his team spent years building the fraud controls and print security that persuaded consumer goods manufacturers, including Procter and Gamble, Unilever and Clorox, to accept digital coupons in place of paper. At CashStar, his co-founder on that board journey was Pete Kledaras, now co-founder and chief technology officer of pmtbox, who built CashStar’s payments and fraud management infrastructure. A notable feature of that platform was acting as the risk-bearing merchant of record for 350 global retailers, absorbing liability for high-risk digital transactions on behalf of clients including The Home Depot and CVS/pharmacy.

That shared history between Boal and Kledaras is central to the announcement. “I was in Maine building CashStar’s payments infrastructure while Steven chaired the company from Mountain View, so I’ve seen how he operates when real money is on the line,” said Kledaras. “Merchants have spent years treating fraud and chargebacks as a cost someone else sets for them, and as an annoying hurdle for consumers. Steven understands why that has to change.”

Boal framed the commercial problem pmtbox is trying to solve in direct terms: most merchants treat payments as a rate negotiated once, then discover that fraud, chargebacks and disputes make the real cost substantially higher, often without realising how conversion rates are simultaneously being eroded.

Market context and regulatory backdrop

The problem pmtbox is addressing is genuine and growing. Card-not-present fraud and chargeback abuse have both risen as digital commerce has expanded, and merchants operating across multiple payment processors and fraud tools routinely lack a unified view of their true transaction economics. The merchant-of-record model that CashStar pioneered is one architectural response; unified commerce platforms that aggregate payments, risk data and dispute management into a single layer are another.

The competitive landscape for merchant payment infrastructure is dense. Stripe, Adyen and Checkout.com each offer risk tooling alongside acquiring, often at scale, while a newer cohort of fraud-specialist vendors competes for the risk intelligence layer separately. For pmtbox, the differentiation claim rests on giving merchants direct control over their own data and economics rather than delegating risk decisions to a processor or gateway. Whether that proposition commands enterprise contract values will depend on the depth of integrations and the loss rates it can demonstrably improve.

In the regulatory dimension, US merchants face ongoing pressure from card scheme chargeback thresholds, and the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau has signalled continued interest in disputes and resolution processes. Any platform that claims to reduce merchant fraud exposure is operating in a space where regulators and card schemes are also actively setting the rules.

Boal currently serves as chief executive and board chair of Matia Mobility, a medical device firm based in Salt Lake City, and has been a guest lecturer at the Stanford Graduate School of Business.

“Our clients are continually looking at new ways to interact and transact with customers, suppliers and business partners,” Tom Lang, PNC’s head of treasury management product and operations, said in a news release. “This solution gives us an opportunity to support our customers with innovative capabilities, backed by the banking experience, risk management and expertise clients expect from PNC.”

The solution builds on PNC’s relationship with Coinbase and the bank’s ongoing investment in its treasury management capabilities, the release said.  It also complements PNC’s faster payments capabilities and is a sign of the bank’s focus on offering clients a “broad range of immediate payment options,” the release added.

“Stablecoins are modernizing how businesses move money by making payments faster, more efficient and more global,” said Alec Lovett, head of infrastructure products at Coinbase. “Our work with PNC shows how leading banks and trusted digital asset infrastructure come together to let corporate clients take advantage of this technology.”

PYMNTS wrote last month that the various possibilities offered by stablecoins are “generating excitement at the highest levels of the payment ecosystem. For example, Mastercard CEO Michael Miebach said recently that cross-border payments are proving to be the strongest use case for the digital tokens.

PYMNTS Intelligence research shows that cross-border B2B transfers are already one of the largest use cases for stablecoins, representing the bulk of global stablecoin payment volume.

“But receiving money is not the same as having spendable working capital,” PYMNTS wrote. “Stablecoins may be creating a faster global payments network without creating a self-sufficient financial system. The more money that network handles, the more consequential its dependence on traditional banking could become.”

Meanwhile, PNC announced last week that it was widening its branch expansion plans to more than 370 new locations by 2031. This figure includes the more 70 branches that have opened since the bank announced its original expansion plans.

This is happening at a moment when “the U.S. bank branch count is moving up meaningfully,” for the first time in years, as “some of the biggest banks are putting billions of dollars behind the physical network,” as PYMNTS wrote in August.

FDIC data shows 69,167 branches at the end of last year, up from 68,632 a year earlier. In addition to PNC, banks such as JPMorgan Chase and Bank of America are in the midst of wide-ranging expansions of their brick-and-mortar footprints.

title: FCA AI Review Prompts Call to Keep Customer Needs Central
snippet: EQWIRE CEO Sophie Njagi urges fintechs to anchor AI product development in customer needs, citing the FCA's latest AI good-practice findings. The post FCA AI Review Prompts Call to Keep Customer Needs Central appeared first on The Fintech Times.
fullText:
The Financial Conduct Authority published its latest review of AI use in financial services this week, identifying examples of good practice alongside areas requiring improvement. The regulator highlighted the importance of defining customer needs before building products, maintaining effective human oversight of AI systems, and ensuring operational resilience. Sophie Njagi, chief executive of UK-regulated Electronic Money Institution EQWIRE, has used the findings to call on fintech businesses to place those principles at the core of product development.

Njagi’s central argument is that commercial enthusiasm for AI is creating a gap between what looks impressive in a product demonstration and what actually serves customers at scale. “Products can look impressive in a demonstration but struggle when customers start using them at scale,” she said. “The test is whether they solve a meaningful problem, make the customer’s experience simpler and have the operations behind them to deliver reliably.”

What the FCA found

The regulator’s review did not name firms but outlined a pattern: financial services businesses are deploying AI tools with insufficient clarity about the customer problem being addressed, and with oversight frameworks that have not kept pace with the capabilities being introduced. Operational resilience, a concept the FCA and Prudential Regulation Authority have embedded in formal rules for several years, featured prominently as an area where AI deployments are lagging.

The findings carry weight in a regulatory environment that is moving quickly. The FCA has signalled a pro-innovation stance on AI but has been equally clear that the Consumer Duty, which came into full force in 2023, requires firms to demonstrate good outcomes for retail customers. That creates a compliance obligation, not merely a design preference, to understand what customers need before committing engineering resource to building.

Five principles for durable product development

Njagi sets out five principles that she argues produce technology products built to last. These cover prioritising genuinely important customer problems over fashionable technology trends; investing in operational foundations rather than surface-layer design; managing complexity internally so customers experience simplicity; building teams with genuine ownership of outcomes; and maintaining the strategic flexibility to change direction as regulation, technology and customer behaviour shift.

The principles are not novel, but the FCA context gives them a compliance dimension that pure product advice lacks. For fintech founders and product leaders, the regulator’s findings amount to a signal that AI roadmaps will receive scrutiny on customer-outcome grounds, not only on technical-risk grounds.

Market context

The FCA review lands in a period of intense AI adoption across retail banking, payments and lending. Established banks and challenger firms alike are integrating large-language-model tooling into customer-facing and back-office processes. The risk the regulator appears most concerned about is the adoption of AI capabilities that are genuinely impressive in controlled conditions but whose performance, edge-case handling and failure modes are not well understood by the firms deploying them.

For smaller fintechs and EMIs operating under tighter capital and compliance resource constraints, the operational resilience requirement is particularly pointed. Building the oversight infrastructure that regulators expect around AI systems adds cost that must be justified by the customer outcome delivered. Njagi’s framing, from the perspective of a CEO running a regulated EMI, is that the discipline required by regulation and the discipline required by good product development are effectively the same thing.

title: COLIBRIX ONE Taps Vivox AI for Automated KYB Merchant Onboarding
snippet: The FCA- and MFSA-authorised payments platform will use Vivox AI's explainable agents to verify corporate documents and run sanctions screening on new merchants. The post COLIBRIX ONE Taps Vivox AI for Automated KYB Merchant Onboarding appeared first on The Fintech Times.
fullText:
COLIBRIX ONE, the payments infrastructure platform operated within the Mellifera group, has selected Vivox AI under a multi-year agreement to automate know-your-business checks across its UK and EU merchant base. The deal is designed to reduce the time compliance analysts spend processing document-heavy due diligence on new business customers without removing human sign-off from the process.

Under the arrangement, Vivox AI’s explainable AI agents will handle corporate document verification, ultimate beneficial owner mapping, and sanctions and adverse media screening. Every AI-generated finding is traceable to its underlying source, and COLIBRIX ONE’s compliance team will review and approve each case before it is closed. The rollout covers merchant onboarding in the UK and EU, with plans to extend to ongoing monitoring and additional entity types in 2027.

What the technology does

Vivox AI’s agents draw on corporate registry data across more than 155 countries to identify ownership structures, shareholders and directors, then generate a full customer due diligence or enhanced due diligence report for analyst review. In an earlier deployment at international payments firm TransferMate, the company said due diligence time fell from roughly 60 minutes to under 15 minutes per case, with screening alerts declining by 86 per cent. Those figures come from Vivox AI’s own account of the TransferMate project and have not been independently verified.

Tim Khamzin, founder and chief executive of Vivox AI, said: “AI agents take on the document-heavy due diligence work where every conclusion comes with a clear audit trail, so analysts stay in control and regulators can see exactly how a decision was reached. That is what makes AI usable in a regulated business.”

COLIBRIX ONE is authorised by the UK Financial Conduct Authority as an electronic money institution (FRN 927920) and holds a parallel authorisation through Mellifera Kartiera Limited from the Malta Financial Services Authority. Its product stack includes card acquiring for one-time and recurring transactions, multi-currency current accounts with dedicated named IBANs, and global payouts, with principal memberships at Visa and Mastercard.

Regulatory and market context

The timing reflects a specific pressure on payment platforms regulated under UK and EU financial crime frameworks. The FCA has tightened its expectations on anti-money laundering controls and merchant due diligence for e-money institutions in recent years, and the EU’s AML package, including the forthcoming AML Authority, will raise baseline obligations further across the bloc. For platforms that compete partly on onboarding speed, manual KYB on merchants with complex, multi-jurisdiction ownership structures is a genuine operational bottleneck.

The market for AI-assisted compliance tooling is expanding quickly. Established regtech vendors and a new generation of AI-native compliance firms are competing to automate the same document-heavy workflows, often positioning explainability and audit-trail quality as the differentiator that makes their products acceptable to risk functions and supervisors alike. COLIBRIX ONE’s choice of a dedicated AI compliance vendor rather than a bundled solution from its existing technology stack reflects a broader pattern among licensed payment firms: separating the compliance workflow layer from the core processing infrastructure in order to swap components as the tooling matures.

The key variable to watch in deployments like this one is whether the efficiency gains cited from the TransferMate reference hold across a larger and more varied merchant portfolio, particularly for merchants with layered holding structures in higher-risk jurisdictions, where beneficial ownership mapping is hardest and regulatory tolerance for errors is lowest.

fullText:
Quantum computing will bring significant opportunities to the UK financial sector, but firms need to act now to prepare for a world where a viable hostile quantum computer could break today’s widely used cryptography standards.

The financial sector depends on secure information and communication. Cryptography – of which encryption is just one part – helps firms protect their clients’ data, verify who they are dealing with, and maintain trust in their systems.

Sufficiently powerful quantum computers pose a real threat to that security. Without trustworthy cryptography, consumers would face fraud, firms would suffer operational disruption, and the integrity of financial transactions and markets would be put at risk.

That’s why we are talking to firms about preparing for post-quantum cryptography (PQC) now. We don’t know for certain when a viable quantum computer will emerge, but the coming years will likely see the technology advance at a rapid pace.

Preparing for this new world requires firms to understand where and how they use cryptography and to be able to migrate all hardware and software to PQC, while managing operational risks.

Realistically, for most firms, this will require significant time, investment and effort.

What firms need to do now

So, what kind of timescale are we talking about? The National Centre for Cyber Security (NCSC) recommends 3 key milestones:

By 2028, firms complete a PQC migration plan.

By 2031, firms carry out high-priority migration activities.

By 2035, firms have migrated all systems, services and products to PQC.

Firms should not wait for these milestones before acting and where it is safe to do so, they should seek to be ready sooner. In line with NCSC guidance, we expect firms to act now to: 

Have a thorough and accurate understanding of the cryptography in place across systems and information.

Set clear, achievable, safe and risk-based migration objectives..

Implement migration plans and monitor, test and validate the changes, adjusting them where necessary.

Senior managers should ensure that their firms allocate enough time, investment and resources to manage PQC migration safely and meet the relevant deadlines. Failed change projects accounted for around a fifth of all incidents reported to us in 2025.

How we are supporting firms

We are trialling a new supervisory self-assessment tool with an initial sample of firms and intend to extend it to other firms in due course. This will help firms assess the maturity of their plans and help us understand the industry’s preparedness for PQC migration.

This trial will also help us identify common challenges and examples of good practice, which we intend to share with the sector.

We shared relevant insights from firms in April 2026 and will continue to engage with the industry through our Cyber Coordination Groups (CCGs), the Cross Market Operational Resilience Group (CMORG), and trade bodies and associations.

We will also consult on cyber resilience guidance for firms, including our expectations for how firms should address PQC risks through their cryptographic controls.

G7 Cyber Expert Group, Statement on advancing a coordinated roadmap for the transition to post-quantum cryptography in the financial sector 

CMORG, Guidance for post-quantum cryptography

title: BNPL for rent seeks a market
snippet: A new crop of fintechs is exploring growth opportunities in pay-later lending for monthly rent payments as inflation pinches consumers.
fullText:
Pay-later loans are increasingly available for monthly housing payments as financial technology companies seek growth by responding to consumers’ affordability struggles.

While the buy now, pay later market has traditionally focused on providing consumers with financing at retail merchants for discretionary items, a newer batch of companies sees profit potential in tailoring loans to rental payments and other monthly bills such as utilities, medical care and telephone service.

A variety of players have moved into the pay-later rental arena in recent years, aiming to fill financial gaps between consumers’ monthly rents and their incomes, as the increases in the former outpace the latter.

Ariel Nelson

Permission granted by National Consumer Law Center

The rise of these businesses is “really revealing in what they say about the state of affordability around life essentials,” said Ariel Nelson, a senior attorney with the National Consumer Law Center. “These products are really appealing because people are desperate.”

Companies seeking to develop a market in the rental area include RealPage, an apartment management software firm, which last year bought Livble, a startup that offers renters flexible payment options. Another is New York-based Flexible Finance, known as Flex, which lets consumers split their rent, mortgage or other monthly bill payments. 

A third rent-focused fintech is Bilt Technologies, which offers a payments and loyalty program aimed at attracting rent and mortgage payments to its co-branded credit cards. In addition to points for rent and everyday spending on its cards, New York-based Bilt issues points for homeowners’ association and condominium fee payments.

Bilt cardholders can transfer the points to 18 airline and seven hotel loyalty partner programs to redeem for flights and hotel stays. The points can also be redeemed at merchants such as Amazon.com and Lyft.

Consumer advocates contend that pay-later products aimed at rent and medical care can exacerbate financial strains for economically vulnerable people and lead to a stacking of their debt.

“As the price of shelter has shot up, a new breed of predatory creditors has emerged aiming to turn this emergency into profit,” advocacy group Protect Borrowers said in a February report on the rent now, pay later industry. “Beneath the surface, these products are united in being little more than a repackaging of an age-old debt trap: payday loans.”

About 109 million Americans have a monthly rental payment, according to Protect Borrowers, a Washington-based nonprofit that lobbies and litigates on consumer debt issues. The group was formed in 2018 as the Student Borrower Protection Center by former officials of the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau. 

Pay-later options allow renters to avoid being late on their rent, avoiding landlords’ late fees and revolving credit card interest rates that can reach 30% or more, Zahir Khoja, RealPage’s chief fintech officer, said in an interview last month. The average late fee is $85, he said.

“It’s not that you can’t pay your rent,” he said of tenant customers that select pay-later plans. “You may not be able to pay your rent on January 1st, and so you need some time in the month of January to be able to do it. It’s much better than paying a late fee or revolving at 29.9 (percent) on credit.”

Another BNPL provider, Sydney-based Zip, offers a bill-payment service to split monthly bills such as insurance, utilities and mobile phone. The company is also exploring a new rent-focused service for the U.S. market. 

Many “everyday Americans” are challenged by a misalignment between the timing of their income and bills, Zip’s U.S. CEO, Joe Heck, told analysts on the BNPL provider’s August earnings call. 

“Most consumers are paid every two weeks, while bills like rent are generally due monthly,” Heck said. “That mismatch in timing of income and expenses creates large opportunities beyond BNPL,” he said, pointing to bill payments and the need for “income-smoothing” as other ways the services could be used. 

Shragie Lichtenstein

Permission granted by Flex

The U.S. monthly rent and bill market is a $2 trillion addressable opportunity, compared to $160 billion for the retail BNPL market, Zip said in its investor presentation.

“I do think that this is a trend, both for rent and in general consumer essentials, that’s likely to continue,” Flex co-founder and CEO Shragie Lichtenstein said in an interview Oct. 8. 

Competing payment plans

RealPage, which is based in suburban Dallas, sells property-management software and rent payment financing services. The company offers both Livble and Flex via its app for residents and property managers or owners. 

Despite its Livble ownership, RealPage promotes both brands with its property owner customers, Khoja said. “We tell them ‘Hey, it’s Pepsi (or) Coke. Let the customer decide which one works for them.’”

Flex is a subscription service for tenants that collects a percentage of the rent as a payment for the service, he said Oct. 18, during an interview at the Money20/20 financial technology conference in Las Vegas. “Whereas ours (Livble) is just a flat fee, so it’s different – whatever works for you better as the resident.”

Another difference is that Flex offers credit cards as a payment method, while Livble accepts only ACH, said Khoja, who joined RealPage in March. 

Livble charges customers a fee for each payment they make, eschewing recurring monthly membership or subscription fees. Livble’s typical payment fee is $30 to $35 but are “nuanced by state,” which is why they’re not posted on the company’s website, a RealPage spokesperson said last week in an email. A resident using Livble, “will always know the fee before it’s final,” the spokesperson said. The company didn’t immediately respond to a question about how it presents its fees to customers. 

“We don’t want you to get into perpetual debt,” Khoja said. “Our goal is to actually help you go up the financial-inclusion ladder, where you’re now able to stand on your own two feet and do things without revolving credit at such high rates or taking third-party loans that you can’t repay.”

A playground at an apartment complex in Irving, Texas, near Dallas.

Getty Images

Two years ago, the Justice Department and eight states filed an antitrust lawsuit alleging that RealPage helped apartment owners collude to fix rental prices. The lawsuit said that the company’s pricing software used nonpublic, sensitive data collected from apartment owners to develop rental rate recommendations in various markets and keep rents higher than they would have been in a competitive market.

The company and government settled the case last year, with RealPage agreeing to stop using sensitive information from landlords to determine the rental prices that it suggested through its software. The company did not admit or deny wrongdoing or face a financial penalty as part of the agreement. Several antitrust lawsuits filed by states and private plaintiffs continue. Private equity firm Thoma Bravo acquired RealPage in 2021. 

Another rent-payment focused startup, New York-based Esusu, has partnered with BNPL provider Affirm Holdings to allow renters to split their rent into two equal payments. The Esusu program remains an “early-stage pilot” in testing and consists only of evenly split rent payments, with no fees or interest, an Affirm spokesperson said last month in an email.

Esusu charges a $59 membership fee, paid monthly or annually, depending on whether a tenant’s apartment property is part of the company’s network. The company also has a “split pay” program allowing renters to pay 60% of their rent upfront and divide the remainder into two or three payments. Esusu did not respond to a message seeking comment on its business model. 

Determining the costs of these rent-payment programs “can be confusing,” said Nelson, the NCLC attorney, noting that such information is often buried deep within user terms and conditions.

“I cannot for the life of me figure out how much they cost,” she said of having looked around different pay-later providers’ websites for pricing information. “And that’s also a problem.”

Scattered regulatory oversight

Pay-later lending has had little oversight at the federal level. Several states – including Illinois, New York and Oregon – have formulated rules to regulate the industry as the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau has contracted during the Trump administration. 

In June, U.S. Rep. Daniel Goldman, a Democrat from New York City, introduced a bill to apply the federal Truth in Lending Act to BNPL loans, effectively regulating them as credit cards. The measure hasn’t moved beyond the House Financial Services Committee, according to Congress’ website.

BNPL “users have been left with no federal protections,” Goldman said in a press release announcing his bill, referring to the CFPB’s decision to retreat last year from a 2024 decision to regulate pay-later loans much like credit cards.

Another bill, filed by Sen. Jack Reed, a Rhode Island Democrat, would amend the Truth in Lending law, which dates to the late 1960s, and the 2010 Consumer Financial Protection Act to apply new oversight and consumer protections. Reed’s legislation, filed late last year, has attracted four Democratic co-sponsors and a companion bill in the House, but no Republican sponsors, according to Congress.gov.

Lichtenstein, the Flex CEO, said that one challenge facing the RNPL industry is that these products “don’t fit into a clean box” neatly for regulators to evaluate what they are and how they work.

“The more you don’t fit into a clean box, the more regulatory scrutiny it draws,” he said. “We have tried our best to fit into a relatively clean box,” he said, adding that the company has “internal guardrails” to help it evaluate “the many, many gray areas that can exist for consumer fintech.”

However, he added, pay-later services for rent differ from other financial services, often “embedded” with the rent payment and with different pricing models. 

The RNPL industry doesn’t currently have a “uniform set of standards” from regulators under which to operate, Lichtenstein said, which can lead to different practices among the various players. “Continued clarity on the right way to do things would be welcome by us,” he said.

Risks for renters?

Beyond high fees and the potential for debt accumulation, rent-payment services pose “a significant risk” to borrowers because lenders often link directly to consumers’ bank accounts and offer “disastrously poor customer service” in addressing errors or other account issues, according to the Protect Borrowers report. 

Their growth is also likely to lead to further regulatory scrutiny, with at least one state, New York, being encouraged by the New York City Department of Consumer and Worker Protection to apply its BNPL rules expansively to other providers in adjacent verticals. 

Pay-later services are marketed by lenders “who claim that these loans can ease the housing affordability or healthcare accessibility crisis,” Commissioner Samuel A.A. Levine of the New York City DCWP wrote in September in a letter to New York state financial regulators. “However, in both cases, these products fail to address the underlying problems and result only in consumers facing new and compounding risks.”

Among various recommendations to the state’s Department of Financial Services, Levine urged regulators to include “all forms of BNPL products” in its pending rules for such lenders, including those that offer rent payment services.

“The stakes are really high, so I think we need to be extremely cautious about how we handle products in this space.”

Ariel Nelson

National Consumer Law Center

Esusu raised $50 million last December. Its platform covers about 5 million rental units, with 12 million people, according to the company’s press release. The company also offers a rent-payment reporting service to help renters build their credit scores. 

Esusu says on its website that its credit services are needed because two-thirds of Americans “live paycheck to paycheck” and that about “30% of lower-income households spend 95% or more of their income on basic necessities like housing, food and utilities.”

Affirm doesn’t allow a consumer to borrow further if they have an outstanding balance from the prior month, Affirm’s vice president of government relations, John Pitts, wrote in a February blog post in response to the Protect Borrowers report, seeking to highlight differences between Affirm and others in the rent market.

“Being financially blindsided by hidden fees and/or still paying January’s rent in March is not solving affordability, it’s stacking debt,” Pitts wrote. “That’s why our products are structurally different.”

Regulators are beginning to “get educated in this space, and they're asking the right questions to provide the consumer protection around it,” said RealPage’s Khoja. Officials in states with the largest numbers of renters – California, Florida, New York and Texas – are among those gathering information about how RNPL firms work, he said.

However, the field of pay later for rent is nascent and state officials are still “catching up” with its growth, said Nelson, the consumer attorney.

“You’re talking about people who are doing whatever it takes to keep a roof over their head,” she said. “This isn’t like I couldn’t pay for an expensive pair of shoes – you could literally be homeless. The stakes are really high, so I think we need to be extremely cautious about how we handle products in this space.”

title: Signicat Names TÜV Austria Sole CAB for eIDAS 2.0 Compliance
snippet: Signicat is consolidating its eIDAS audits under a single conformity assessment body, replacing a five-CAB structure built up through acquisitions. The post Signicat Names TÜV Austria Sole CAB for eIDAS 2.0 Compliance appeared first on The Fintech Times.
fullText:
Signicat, the Norwegian digital identity provider, has appointed TÜV Austria as its sole Conformity Assessment Body (CAB) for all eIDAS-related audits, replacing a fragmented arrangement in which five separate CABs assessed different parts of its business. The consolidation, announced on 20 October 2026, is a direct consequence of the company’s M&A-driven expansion and the growing regulatory demands of eIDAS 2.0.

The company’s acquisition trail had left it with compliance assessments spread across multiple bodies in different European jurisdictions. That structure added administrative overhead and made it harder for customers in regulated sectors, primarily banking, insurance and financial services, to get a coherent picture of Signicat’s compliance posture across its full service catalogue.

Why a single CAB matters under eIDAS 2.0

The timing of the consolidation is not incidental. The revised eIDAS regulation, eIDAS 2.0, establishes the framework for the EU Digital Identity Wallet and places new conformity assessment obligations on trust service providers. Signicat is already a participant in several of the EU’s large-scale wallet pilots, including WE BUILD, Aptitude, NOBID and EWC. Operating under a single CAB simplifies the audit trail as wallet interoperability standards are formalised, and makes it easier to combine eIDAS assessments with adjacent certifications such as ISO 27001 and SOC 2.

Jon Ølnes, VP of digital Identity and regulation at Signicat, said the company ran a formal request-for-information process among its existing CABs before selecting TÜV Austria. “We decided to run an RFI among the CABs and TÜV Austria had the best solutions and services to consolidate the situation and for the changes ahead as EUDI Wallets are introduced across Europe.”

TÜV Austria already assessed Signicat’s identity proofing service, giving it an existing baseline of the company’s technical environment. The transition to single-CAB coverage will be phased to avoid gaps in continuous compliance, according to the company.

Market and regulatory context

The consolidation reflects a broader maturation dynamic in the European digital identity sector. The European Commission has targeted adoption of an EU Digital Identity Wallet by 80 per cent of EU citizens by 2030, a target that is driving commercial demand for verifiable trust services and pushing providers to demonstrate audit-grade compliance at scale. Juniper Research has estimated the global digital identity market will reach 80 billion dollars by the same year, though such long-range market sizing projections carry wide uncertainty.

For Signicat’s bank and fintech customers, the practical benefit is transparency. A single CAB produces a unified compliance view that aligns more naturally with how regulated financial institutions conduct their own third-party due diligence. Banks operating under the EU’s Digital Operational Resilience Act, which came into full effect in January 2025, face stricter obligations around the oversight of critical technology suppliers, and a cleaner audit structure from a supplier reduces friction in that process.

fullText:
Amazon is observing the second anniversary of its “Haul” discount store amid a surge in customer adoption.

The company announced Monday (Nov. 9) its week-long “early Haul-iday” event, featuring things like “$1 flash deals” all week and millions of products priced under $10, along with exclusive “$0.11 steals” on Nov. 10 and 11.

“We’ve always focused on offering customers the lowest prices across the widest selection, and Amazon Haul is another way we’re making holiday shopping more affordable,” said David Forsythe, vice president of Amazon’s North American seller business.

“Whether customers are decorating their homes, dressing the family for festivities, hosting a holiday gathering, or filling up stockings, there’s so much to discover on Amazon Haul, with millions of products at ultra-low prices and new deals dropping all season long,” Forsythe added.

The announcement noted the rapid pace of customer adoption, with the number of people making purchases via Haul increasing by almost 350% year over year. Amazon is also expanding the marketplace’s selection by more than 25 times to upwards of 10 million products.

This is happening at a time when—as PYMNTS wrote last week—“Black Friday has developed a scheduling problem,” as it “keeps arriving before Friday.”

Black Friday falls on Nov. 27 this year, with Cyber Monday following on Nov. 30. All the same, “retailers are already warming up the discount machinery,” the report said. “With Amazon and Walmart running sales events throughout the year, it’s reasonable to wonder how much distinction remains in the Thanksgiving shopping ritual. Quite a lot, judging by the spending.”

Adobe’s numbers for last year’s holiday season placed online Black Friday purchases in the United States at $11.8 billion, up 9.1% from 2024. Cyber Monday came to $14.25 billion,  the year’s biggest day for online shopping.

Frequent promotions have given shoppers more occasions to spend, while these two dates still “concentrate substantial demand,” the report said. “What’s changing is the calendar, the access rules and, occasionally, the merchandise.”

Walmart’s holiday schedule includes Early Black Friday Deals Nov. 12-15, Black Friday Deals Nov. 23-29 and Cyber Monday offers Nov. 30-Dec. 2, with select deals for Walmart+ members.

Target’s Early Black Friday Sale took place last week, while Amazon is hoping to entice shoppers with early deals prior to Black Friday.

“The implication for merchants is straightforward,” PYMNTS wrote. “Waiting until Thanksgiving risks arriving after customers have allocated their budgets. Black Friday has become a rolling competition to capture the purchase first.”

title: Boost Payment Solutions Partners Airwallex for Cross-Border B2B Cards
snippet: Boost says payment volume processed through Airwallex grew nearly ten-fold in five months, with 270 international supplier accounts onboarded. The post Boost Payment Solutions Partners Airwallex for Cross-Border B2B Cards appeared first on The Fintech Times.
fullText:
Boost Payment Solutions has formalised a commercial partnership with Airwallex, under which the Melbourne-founded fintech provides global processing and acquiring infrastructure for Boost’s B2B card payments business. The arrangement has been running for five months and, according to both companies, has already delivered a near ten-fold increase in payment volume processed through the Airwallex rails, alongside the onboarding of more than 270 international supplier accounts.

Dean M. Leavitt, founder and CEO at Boost Payment Solutions

The partnership targets a structural pain point in cross-border B2B card acceptance. When a buying enterprise wants to pay an international supplier by commercial card, the friction typically lands on the supplier side: slow onboarding, elevated failure rates, retry loops that delay settlement, and processing costs that make wire transfer look more attractive. Boost says the integration addresses each of those: suppliers can go live in as few as two business days, payment failure rates are lower, and eligible high-value transactions are routed to qualify for large-ticket interchange rates. European flows are also said to benefit from optimised scheme fees.

Dean M. Leavitt, founder and chief executive of Boost Payment Solutions, said the partnership was about infrastructure consistency at scale. “Global B2B payments shouldn’t become more complicated simply because a business crosses a border,” he said. “By combining their global processing capabilities with our specialised B2B expertise, we can continue raising the bar for the customers and suppliers we serve.”

The commercial logic

The division of labour is legible. Airwallex holds more than 85 licences across North and Latin America, Europe, the Middle East and Asia-Pacific, giving it a regulated acquiring footprint that would take years and significant capital to replicate independently. Boost, founded in New York in 2009 and active in more than 180 countries, brings proprietary technology for large-ticket card optimisation and the supplier-side commercial relationships that acquiring infrastructure alone cannot provide. Neither company disclosed revenue figures, processing volumes in absolute terms, or the commercial structure of the arrangement.

The “nearly ten-fold” volume growth figure is notable but should be read in context. A ten-fold increase from a low base can be achieved quickly during an active onboarding push; the more durable signal will be retention rates among those 270-plus suppliers and whether average transaction values justify the large-ticket interchange positioning.

Market context and regulatory read-across

The B2B cross-border card market is undergoing sustained structural change. Historically dominated by wire transfers and paper cheque, it has been shifting toward card-based and virtual card programmes as buyers seek the working-capital float, rebate income and data enrichment that cards provide. Several infrastructure providers, including Convera, Nuvei and Flywire among others, compete for the large-ticket B2B acquiring segment, while banking-as-a-service layers increasingly enter from below.

Regulatory tailwinds and headwinds are both in play. The European interchange caps introduced under the Interchange Fee Regulation have compressed margin on consumer card flows, making B2B and commercial card corridors proportionally more attractive to acquirers. At the same time, PSD3 and the forthcoming Payment Services Regulation in the EU are expected to sharpen rules around cross-border payment transparency and failure-rate disclosure, which could raise the bar for the kind of performance claims Boost and Airwallex are making in this release.

Airwallex’s licence count and dual headquarters in San Francisco and Singapore reflect a deliberate strategy to be domestically regulated in major corridors rather than relying on passporting. That approach becomes more commercially durable as regulators worldwide move away from light-touch treatment of non-bank payment firms. For Boost, the partnership is a way to inherit that regulatory infrastructure without bearing the full compliance overhead internally. The next milestone to watch is whether the partnership is extended to additional acquiring markets or whether Boost eventually seeks its own acquiring licences in key corridors.

Dive Brief:

First Citizens Bank is partnering with NCR Atleos to offer surcharge-free access to services via ATMs located at some 2,000 Target stores, the bank said in a press release last month. As part of the agreement, the bank’s customers can use the ATMs at Target stores to withdraw cash, check their account balances and transfer funds to eligible linked accounts without paying a fee, according to the Oct. 19 release.

“The consumer banking experience needs to meet customers where they are through multiple channels, whether in-person or digitally enabled,” First Citizens Bank’s head of consumer banking, Michael Wilson, said in the release. 

Meanwhile, NCR Atleos CEO Tim Oliver said Wednesday that the company’s sale to Brink’s is progressing, with expected completion of the transaction by January.

Dive Insight:

For NCR Atleos, which became a standalone company three years ago, the partnership with First Citizens allows it to add new service providers to its roster. 

The company separated from its parent in late 2023, creating two publicly traded companies: NCR Voyix and NCR Atleos. While NCR Atleos offers ATMs and other interactive teller machines for payments and banking services, NCR Voyix offers point-of-sale hardware and related services to restaurant, retail and other merchants.

As NCR Atleos has grown its corporate clientele, including by working with American Express and PayNearMe in recent years, its self-service banking segment has bolstered revenue. The company reported third-quarter earnings results Wednesday that showed its self-service banking segment rose 3% to $2.17 billion for the first nine months of the year, faster than its overall business revenue growth, which increased 2% to $3.23 billion for the period, according to the earnings press release. 

“Our service-led growth initiatives and investment in product innovation are encouraging financial institutions and retailers to choose our differentiated and comprehensive offering to meet their evolving self-service needs,” Oliver said in August when the company reported second-quarter earnings. 

NCR’s partnership with First Citizens comes as the ATM provider prepares to be acquired. In February, the Brink’s Company agreed to buy NCR Atleos in a cash and stock transaction valued at about $6.6 billion. As part of the deal, Brink’s will also take on $2.6 billion in NCR Atleos debt, a press release on the transaction said. 

Regulators have yet to approve the deal. The Competition and Markets Authority in the U.K. said Brink’s acquisition of NCR Atleos could limit competition, according to a September report from the news outlet Reuters. Earlier this month, the Wall Street Journal reported Brink’s plans to sell some subsidiaries in a move aimed at assuaging U.K. concerns.

“We continue to make meaningful progress on regulatory approval processes across the multiple jurisdictions, and have significantly advanced the integration planning activities for the pending combination of Atleos and The Brink’s Company,” Oliver said in the release this week.

title: FIS, Toast CFOs exit
snippet: The chief financial officers are leaving the payments players as the companies grapple with separate challenges.
fullText:
Fidelity National Information Services and Toast separately disclosed that their chief financial officers are exiting, as they also announced third-quarter earnings results. 

At FIS, which provides payments services to banking and capital markets clients, the company announced the departure of James Kehoe, with no further explanation. Alexandra “Alex” Brooks will step into the CFO post on an interim basis starting Thursday as the company begins a search for a permanent replacement, according to a Wednesday press release.

The CFO change at Jacksonville, Florida-based FIS landed as the company adjusted its financial forecasts due to unexpected changes in the outlook for recurring revenue, citing new factors that are dragging on that income.

The shifts were mainly related to changed expectations at some of its banking clients as those customers encounter implementation delays and, in some cases, work through acquisition activity, CEO Stephanie Ferris explained on a webcast with analysts Wednesday. The change is happening as some customers move from services with more traditional licenses to the company’s more updated subscription software services, she said.

“Over the course of the third quarter, we started to see some client-directed conversion delays, primarily in our larger client base, and some impacts from the timing around large bank consolidation,” Ferris said on the webcast.

FIS divests prepaid business

She also noted that the company would invest in technology and security to assist clients with implementations and to prioritize cyber work.

“These factors will weigh on our results in the fourth quarter in 2027, and we expect them to largely fade in 2028,” Ferris said. 

FIS also disclosed during the third-quarter report that it had sold what it referred to as a “non-core, prepaid asset” for $100 million. A spokesperson for the company didn’t immediately respond to requests for more information about the unit or the buyer.

Kehoe has been with FIS since August 2023, joining shortly after Ferris became CEO in January of that year. Together, they took the company through a $24.25 billion sale last year of its merchants services business Worldpay to Global Payments, and the $13.5 billion acquisition of a card issuer business from Global Payments.

FIS reported third-quarter adjusted net earnings rose 5.3% to $831 million as operating revenue climbed 29%, on an adjusted basis, to $3.37 billion, according to the company’s earnings press release.

At Toast, the digital payments processor said that its president and chief financial officer, Elena Gomez, will leave her posts at the end of the year. Michael Senno, who has served as Toast’s senior vice president of finance, will become CFO at that time, the company said.

Gomez, who has been at Toast since May 2021 and guided the company through its initial public offering that year, said in the company’s earnings press release that it’s time “to take a break before my next chapter.”

Toast CEO criticizes lawsuit

Meanwhile, during a webcast with analysts on Tuesday, Toast’s CEO, Aman Narang, continued to make a case for fighting a lawsuit brought by the Federal Trade Commission and states last week. The federal and state regulators alleged in their lawsuit that the company exacted “hidden fees” and “unauthorized charges” from both merchants and consumers. 

Narang defended the contracts Toast negotiates with every restaurant, and other merchants, to provide services in the business-to-business industry. 

The lawsuit turns on the Federal Trade Commission Act and the Restore Online Shoppers’ Confidence Act, barring companies from misleading customers. The regulators said Toast made “false or misleading claims” regarding its subscription and financing services; failed to make required disclosures; didn’t provide simple ways for customers to cancel their subscription; and charged customers without their consent. 

“We are incredibly disappointed with the FTC's decision to file the suit,” Narang told analysts on the earnings webcast. “We've been engaged with them and cooperating with them really over the past year, and fundamentally believe their application of ROSCA is unprecedented for custom contracts in B2B.”

Narang posited that the enforcement action on that basis could impact the entire industry. “If ROSCA were to apply to B2B custom negotiated contracts in a B2B context, it would have huge implications for, really, the whole industry and business contracts in general,” Narang contended. “We have a lot of confidence in our business practices and are ready to defend ourselves.” 

Toast reported third-quarter net income rose 60% to $169 million as revenue increased 21% to $1.98 billion, according to the earnings press release.

The CFOs at both FIS and Toast said they’ll continue to work with the companies to transfer their duties to their successors.
